speechtext: That a message be sent to the Senate requesting that their Honours will give leave to the Hon. Archibald B. McCoig, one of their members, to attend and give evidence before the Seleot Standing Committee on Agriculture and Colonization.

This motion, Mr. Speaker, is
for the purpose of securing the attendance of the Hon. Mr. McCoig before the committee in order to examine him on the standardization of repair parts for agricultural implements, a matter not yet before the committee, but we wish to take it up at a later date.

in order for a motion to be made on behalf of the Committee on Agriculture without a report from that committee being first presented.

speechtext:
(Centre Vancouver) :	This matter was discussed in
the committee, and unquestionably it should be part of the report of the committee's proceedings. Why a report has not been presented to-day in the usual manner is, I think, a fit subject of inquiry. The rules of the House require that a report should be presented. None was presented when the appropriate order was called.

maintopic: MOTION FOR ATTENDANCE OF SENATOR McOOIG
speechtext:
I
think in this case, Mr. Speaker, opposition to the motion should be withdrawn. I understand it is the intention of the committee to investigate the standardization of repair parts for farm implements. Senator McCoig has given the matter a lifelong study and probably is as well informed in regard to it as any man in this Parliament. I understand he is willing to attend and give evidence, and, if so, I see no reason why any technical objection should be raised by my hon. friend for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). I think the motion might very well be adopted and so expedite investigation of this very important matter.

maintopic: MOTION FOR ATTENDANCE OF SENATOR McOOIG
speechtext:
My hon. friend from
Marquette (Mr. Crerar) wholly misunderstands me. I wish to submit this to you, Mr. Speaker, as a point of order. The subject matter of this resolution was discussed in the committee to-day. In the ordinary course it should form part of the committee's report. I have absolutely no objection to the motion, except that I cannot understand why the ordinary procedure was departed from and no report presented to the House; at least, I have not been able to learn of any up to this moment. I submit, Sir, that this resolution cannot possibly
be moved until a report of the committee incorporating this resolution is submitted to the House.

Licenses to manufacture oleomargarine shall

speechtext: I beg to move, in accordance with notice given, that when the House adjourns on Tuesday, May 23rd, it stand adjourned until Friday, May 26.

I would suggest to the leader of the Government that we adjourn until the following Monday. That would make it possible for those hon. members, who do not want to hang around Ottawa for two days, to go home.
I suggest that we sit on Saturday.

I dissent from the suggestion of my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Hocken). There are a good many members of the House from the maritime provinces and the far West who are desirous of having the business expedited as rapidly as possible. It is only a few hours journey to Toronto, where my hon. friend lives, and he can doubtless go home on Tuesday evening and return on Friday.

If the idea is to conserve time, then I think that we might sit Wednesday nights and on Saturdays as well. I am perfectly satisfied to stay here all the time if hon. members are anxious to get the business of the House done. Let us adjourn over the 24th and come back on Thursday.
Motion agreed to.

Mr. MITiC/HEiLL: In view of some of the criticims that have been directed to certain members on this side, including m self, as to the stand we took during the last electoral campaign, in view of the statement made by the Government in the Speech from the Throne to the effect that they intended to give public operation of railways a fair trial, and finally in view of the statement made by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Kennedy) on the eleventh of last month, I feel that it is my duty to discuss the position maintained by us at that time. I may say that my position upon that question has not changed. I am still of the opinion that I was before and during the campaign; but in view of the statement that has been made by the Minister of Railways I feel that I owe some explanation, not only to the House but to my constituency and to the people of my native province where I discussed this question very freely. I realize and understand that there are many hon. members of this House, and many men throughout the country, who do not agree with the position I took during that campaign, which was to the effect that I was against public ownership and operation of railways. I have no quarrel with those who disagree with me upon this matter; they are entitled to their opinion. I respect (their view fully, but I ask them to give the same thought to my own-an i op inion

Supply-Railways
which I can assure the House has been reached after having given a great deal of honest and sincere consideration to the question and after having studied the matter in all its aspects.
Let us endeavour, if we can, to discuss the question freely and frankly, entirely apart from all bitterness of any kind, because, to my mind, it is not a political issue and should not so be considered; it is too serious for that. It is a question which I think, should be looked upon as a national issue because, if I am right in my beliefs with respect to it, it is a danger to the very credit of our country. In saying that I only reiterate what I said during the last election campaign. In saying that I took into consideration then, and take into consideration now, the vast area of our country; I took into consideration our sparse population; I took into consideration the development that has taken place in Canada; I took into consideration the enormous debt that we have and I took into consideration the fact, as I believe, that we are taxed pretty nearly to the limit. Taking all these elements into consideration I stated then, and I state now, that I do not believe our country can stand a deficit of $72,000,000 a year-even if it is only that, and I expect to be able to show that there will be a far greater deficit on the operation of our railways during the past year. In order that there shall be no misunderstanding about the position I took upon this question during the last electoral campaign, allow me to read from the remarks I made when I accepted the nomination for St. Antoine division at the very beginning of the campaign. This is one of the most important matters that this committee has to consider. I listened with very much interest to the remarks made by my hon. friend from St. Antoine (Mr. Mitchell). He stated quite frankly that he did not believe in the public ownership of public utilities, and he expressed very clearly his view that government ownership of such utilities could not possibly be made a success. I have no quarrel with the view entertained by my hon. friend. I recognize that there are in this House and outside many people who do not believe in public ownership, and I respect their view. I think they hold that view as honestly as I do the opposite view, that certain public utilities from their very nature are natural monopolies that can be administered by public agencies with better advantage to the public weal.
This is a question of the very greatest importance, because it touches the whole

subject of transportation, and when we consider the physical character of this country and the scattered nature of its population, we at once realize that there is no subject of such great moment to our people as cheap and reasonable transportation facilities. For that reason, if for no other, the subject is of the very greatest importance. But it is particularly important to us at the present time because of the financial considerations involved. Had it not been for the very great increase in our national debt resulting from the part we took in the war, our railway problem, serious as it is, would not have been by any means beyond our capacity to handle readily and easily without our scarcely feeling the burden. But I quite agree writh my hon. friend from St. Antoine that the existing situation, by reason of the enormous debt that this country has to carry, is one that must command the most serious and earnest consideration of this House and the country.
I quite realize the effect that sustained heavy deficits On the operation of our national railways may have upon our national credit. I cannot agree with my hon. friend, however, in the doleful picture he has drawn that if we do not get rid of these deficits immediately our national credit will go to pieces and we will be in a very bad way indeed. We have had these deficits for several years past, they are a matter of common knowledge not only in Canada but in the countries ih which Canada borrows her money; but as my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Hocken) has pointed out, it has not affected the interest rate on our loans. A few weeks ago my hon. friend, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) negotiated a large loan in the city of New York. That loan was oversubscribed in a few hours' time. I think it was one of the most striking evidences we could possibly have as to the innate soundness of Canada's financial position.
The question we have to consider is hoiw we can best handle this whole proposition, and before I address myself to a consideration of that question I want to offer a word of criticism of those who condemn the public administration of these railways, including my hon. friend from St. Antoine. We have those in the House and those outside who attribute all the difficulties we are in financially from our being in the business of operating railways, and they say that government ownership and operation can never succeed and we should get rid of these railways at once.

There may he some criticism offered that in the arbitration of the value of the common stock of the Canadian Northern Railway, a sum of money was paid to the promoters, to which they were not entitled. But that does not affect the substance of my argument at all. There was no other course for this country to follow than the taking over of this railway system. And the same thing applies just as fully to the Grand Trunk Pacific. Why was the National Transcontinental and whole Grand Trunk Pacific enterprise undertaken? It was undertaken first at the suggestion of the Grand Trunk Railway. I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), who was in the government of the day, will bear me out in this respect, that it was the officials of the Grand Trunk Railway who first approached the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier away back in 1902 or 1903 and asked for assistance in building the transcontinental line that would go into the prairie regions of the West. That was where the suggestion first came from. The Canadian government, with the full approval and consent of the Canadian people, undertook that enterprise. The government built the Transcontinental from Moncton to Winnipeg. By bond guarantees of a very liberal amount, it assisted the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific in the prairie regions and through the mountains of northern British Columbia. All that assistance was given and guaranteed by the government. What different course should have been followed when the officials of the Grand Trunk Pacific, in March, 1918, notified the government of the day that unless they got further subsidies in cash they would close down the operations of the road because they could not pay the running expenses? There was no other course for the government of the day to follow than the course it did follow. Tens of thousands of settlers had gone in along the road and were dependent on the railway for their means of communication. Towns

had sprung up which were in the same position. What would have happened if the road had ceased operations? My hon. friends ask again: Why did you not let it go into the hands of the receiver? Would that have repaid the people for the $50,000 a mile bond guarantees they had given in northern British Columbia? There was only one business course to follow, and that was to secure the roads, link them into the whole national system of railways, and build upon that system for the future, recognizing their great potential value and hoping eventually to emerge successfully from the difficulty. I might add, in passing, that the assistance that was given to the Grand Trunk Pacific totalled $114,000,000.
Now, there has been a good deal of criticism of the late government in regard to this matter. I am referring to the subject not in order to provoke questions of controversy, but because I think that this aspect of the matter should be placed before the public. There has been a good deal of criticism of the late government in acquiring the old Grand Trunk. The situation in that respect is well known. The Grand Trunk desired to evade their responsibilities in connection with the Grand Trunk Pacific, which was their subsidiary company. The government recognized that, in view of the fact that this whole enterprise, which had committed Canada to hundreds of millions of dollars, had been undertaken at the request of the Grand Trunk Kailway, the obligation of the Grand Trunk in respect to the Grand Trunk Pacific could not be thrown aside. What course, then, was open to the government? It is a matter of common knowledge that they adopted the only wise course possible in the circumstances. There was nothing facing the old Grand Trunk Railway but absolute and complete bankruptcy, and it would have gone into the hands of the receiver and have been knocked down under the hammer to the highest bidder. But what would have happened if, in that event, the Grand Trunk had passed into the hands of the Canadian Pacific Railway or of some other private concern, that would not have been willing to make the necessary traffic arrangements with the Transcontinental system? The whole National Transcontinental system, the Grand Trunk Pacific system, was built entirely upon the assumption that it would be linked up with and be part of the Grand Trunk system in eastern Canada. If it

was necessary in 1903 to create a system of that kind, was it not just as necessary in 1917 or 1918 to maintain the principle that lay behind the whole enterprise in 1903? There was no other course to be followed. The Grand Trunk system had to be brought into the Canadian National system, and the government of that day, in my judgment, would have been derelict in their duty if they had failed to do so. There are many things upon which I have differed with my right hon. friend who leads the Opposition (Mr. Meighen), and I suppose that in our public careers in the future there will still be many points of difference between us. But I believe that the policy of the late government in respect of the whole railway question in its main essentials was the only sound policy this country could follow; and for that reason I consistently supported it.

I lay this down. I
think you can attract to a great national enterprise of this kind the brains, the ability and the spirit of public service that will make it a success, but you can never do it under the system that obtained on the Intercolonial when it was a department of the government, because then it was frankly and openly under government control.
It was run with surpluses.

That may or may not
be the case. I do not think my hon. friend's statement can be borne out by an examination of the facts.

Mr. Cochrane, in 1913, when he was Minister of Railways, gave to the House a statement of the operation of that railway for five years, during which the railway showed a net surplus of $1,000,000 in operation.
It may be true that during a few years-
Not a few years, a great number of years.

Well, for quite a number of years, but I would point out to my hon. friend that from the time it was built right up to the present there was never

a cent of interest charged against that investment.

Neither
was there against the canals of this country; they were built under the same conditions.
Very true, but if you are going to operate the Intercolonial on that basis-
Not at all.

My hon. friend is entitled to his opinion, and will have an opportunity to speak later on if he wishes to do so. I repeat, it is possible to attract to the management of a great public enterprise of this kind the brains and ability and the spirit of public service that will make it a success. I am convinced it can be done, and I trust that that is the intention and desire of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways, and the Government when they select their board. Let me say in passing that when they select their board, the men should be in sympathy with the whole proposition, so far as it is possible to get such men. We have had the suggestion from my hon. friend from St. Antoine that it is necessary to travel to Europe or the United States or Africa or somewhere else to find supermen, if such can be found, to handle this system. My experience in business, Mr. Chairman, running over a good many years, has led me to the conclusion that supermen are very difficult to find, and very often they are not of very great consequence after you have found them. This system will never be saved by supermen-never-but I am convinced you can find right in Canada, possibly in the system itself, men who have the potential ability and capacity to handle this thing.

Will the hon. member express it as his opinion that Mr. Hanna or Mr. Mitchell, who I understand are the only two directors from the old system, were in the least degree responsible for the inability of the Canadian Northern to finance itself?

I would venture the
opinion so far as my knowledge goes that they were not, but that is not germane to the argument I am making. I am asserting that the ability and the capacity to handle the system can be found in Canada.
There is one other thing that is necessary if the system is to be made a success. You

Supply-Railways
must enlist public support behind it, and that can be done. I think it is possible to have this great national enterprise recognized by the people of Canada as a great national asset, an asset in which they can take pride, a thing that will help to link up this country and unify it. I believe that is possible, but it is not possible if political considerations enter into the management and control-if sectional considerations, whether west, east, middle, or anywhere else, enter into the direction and management of the system. Under those circumstances I do not believe it is possible to make it a success.
Reference was made the other night to a contract for steel rails that was let in the month of October last, and my hon. friend from St. Antoine paid some attention to it this afternoon. I think that the late administration can be fairly criticized in respect to that contract. The business of the National Railways in respect to contracts of all kinds should be put upon an absolutely definite business basis, and no considerations other than the soundest business principles should govern. If your national system of railways is to be used to advance the interests of any one section by giving employment to labour, or by letting contracts to companies who may want business, it is not upon a sound basis, the system cannot succeed in this manner, and so far as I am concerned I shall criticise and continue to criticise that method of administration of these roads.

If by giving these contracts to private companies you could save a large amount of money to the treasury, would the hon. member not be in favour of placing the contracts where the work could be done most cheaply? If it can be shown, for instance, that cars can be repaired in a private concern, where perhaps the McAdoo wage scale does not apply, for a hundred dollars less per car than in the government shops, would he still advocate that the work be done in the government shops?

I regret that I failed to make myself clear to my hon. friend. I say that one consideration that should govern in the control of these railways is, having regard to all the factors of the case, to have the business done where it can be done most cheaply. I do not care where it is done, but no consideration other than that should govern.
Hear, hear.
Now, I want to say a word or two as to some of the things which in my judgment are essential.

If the statement made by the hon. member for Cumberland is correct, that cars can be repaired, or any work done, very much cheaper in private shops than the same work can be done for in the government shops would not that be a very strong argument against public ownership and operation? If the statement is true it is a serious matter.

I am not assuming, Mr. Chairman, that my hon. friend from Cumberland is correct in his facts but I do say this: If it could be done more cheaply there I would have it done there; there are many concerns that are in the business of doing this kind of work, that is their business. But that is a totally different thing, and upon a totally different basis from the operation of a great enterprise which is in the nature of a natural monopoly. That is the point of my argument, because there is no one in this House more strongly opposed to government interference in things which in their very nature are matters of private business than I am, because in such things people can best act for themselves; but in a great national enterprise like this, where you can only have one line of railway you must have either very rigid control of your system if the public are to be protected or it must be a vehicle owned and operated by the people as a whole through their government.
Now when my hon. friend interrupted me I was about to remark there are some other things that are essential to the success of this operation. I have suggested in the House before, and I again offer the suggestion to the minister, that when this unification takes place, and your board is selected, there should be a complete revaluation of the whole national system of railways. I think there can be little doubt that these roads to-day as an operating concern are not worth the amount of money that they stand in our books at, and they are not worth that amount because of the very manner in which they were built. I will give the House a case which illustrates the point I am making. West of Edmonton, running through the Yellowhead pass, the Canadian Northern Railway built its lines to the point where the railway turns down the North Thompson river to the Fraser river. Through that same pass was constructed the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway. Those two lines of railway
Supply-Railways

travelled for scores, yes, hundreds, of miles almost always within sight of each other, and indeed for many miles the tracks were so close together that they appeared to be a double track. During the war, when these railways were consolidated, it was necessary to lift the rails of a portion of one of these lines to send to the front. I know there has been some criticism of that action but that does not alfect the point of my illustration. You can travel, Sir, over that line to-day and see the scores, yes, hundreds, of miles of railways that have been abandoned. The Grand Trunk Pacific railway is on one side of the pass, and the old Canadian Northern right of way on the other side, and there have been hundreds of miles of track abandoned ifhioh were of the most difficult and costly construction. You can travel there and see the wreck of a railway: Iron bridges, tunnels, rock cuts, all this sort of thing, upon which no rails are laid at the present time, and upon which I venture to say none ever will be laid; and yet that expensive mileage, costing, I believe, something in the neighbourhood of $100,000 a mile, stands in the books of the Government as a part of the value of the assets of this concern. There should, therefore, be a complete re-valuation of the system so as to put it down to a sound business basis, following precisely the same practice that a merchant follows when he finds he has goods on the shelf that have deteriorated in quality, and he must write them down and take his loss. That should be done in the case of this railway system. You cannot get a management, I care not how efficient or how able they may be, who will tackle a problem of that kind with the vigour, the energy and the willingness that is necessary, if they feel that they have to make headway against a heavy handicap of that kind.
You think good headway would then be made?

Yes, because it is a
sound business practice and for that reason I commend it to the Government. If we have a capital loss in the construction of these railways let us face it frankly and put it where it belongs-add it to the debt of Canada. Do not let it stand against the system, otherwise you wil prejudice the cause of public ownership from one end of the country to the other, and it will be said "How can you make your railways pay when you are operating
tMr. Crerar.]
under conditions which render it practically impossible for them to do so?"
There is one other suggestion I have to make and that is in reference to the question of immigration. I agree with the view-

My hon. friend has been discussing a very interesting matter, and I would like to question him further in regard to it. As to the revaluation of the government railway property, would he be favourable to revalueing at an operating profit value or on a replacement basis?
I think a proper basis to take would be the basis of replacement under fair conditions.
I am afraid that would increase the valuation.

My hon. friend suggests that the railways should be re-valued and the amounts covering the properties which have been apportioned should be written off. Does he suggest that the interest on the bonds, or any other obligation which covers the cost of construction, which is no longer in existence, should be no longer chargeable and help to make up the deficits on the operation of the roads?
I am very grateful to my hon. friend from South Waterloo who has made the point clearer than I made it myself.
Is it not a mere question of book-keeping, and the railway situation is not changed at all?

It may be as far as the net result to the country as a whole is concerned; but I am advocating this because of its effect upon the management of your system. That is the reason, and the only reason, that could be advanced in favour of it. My right hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) suggests that it might lead to an increase in value of the system to act on the basis I suggested. I do not think he is correct in that. I was going to elaborate that point further. We have, for instance, three national transcontinental lines running through practically a thousand miles of wilderness between Ontario and Manitoba. I do not know how far I may be correct, but I certainly think it would be the duty of the management to give due consideration to the closing up of a portion of these lines. We have the same thing in the West where there is duplication of services. All these factors should be taken into account in arriving at a proper basis of operations.

Supply-Railways
I want now to pass on to the question of immigration and I agree with the remarks made by my hon. friend from St. Antoine in this respect, that the question of immigration has a very important hearing upon the ultimate success of these roads. The difficulty with our railway situation is that we are overbuilt with railways in Canada, and the only final solution of the matter-and I submit a solution can only be found in a long view of the situation-is in getting more people into the country, by a policy that will bring in immigrants by tens of thousands or scores of thousands, and it should be directed to placing those immigrants along the lines of the National system, because, when you place them along that line, particularly in western Canada, you put them in the best portions of the country, where there will he the greatest likelihood of their making a success. Not only are you ensuring success for them, but you are creating 'business potentially for your roads.
Is it not a fact that a great portion of those lands are now in the hands of private companies?

I think the statement of the hon. member from Dorchester (Mr. Cannon) is true. I do not know the exact acreage in the hands of private companies. We find in western Canada, on account of the supertaxes imposed by the provincial governments on speculative holdings of land, that there is a very general disposition on the part of private owners to sell their lands at reasonable prices. There are still some homestead lands left, but I submit that, as far as possible, the Government should direct the settlement of the immigration to this country to districts that will provide business for the National Railways.
I am not going at the moment to touch that much contested question, the Tariff, but I think that the fiscal policy of this country has a great hearing on this problem. I hope that my hon. friend, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) when he comes to consider his budget will have regard to that. I have stated before in this House and outside that agriculture is the real foundation of the prosperity of the Dominion, and when I examine the traffic returns of the railways, I find the greatest contribution in tonnage to our railways comes from farms, forests and mines. Let me give some information to the committee in that regard, and my figures are taken from the annual railway report.
Taking the Canadian Northern Railway, for the year ending 1920 the farms contributed over 4,000,000 tons, or 28 per cent of the freight hauled over the Canadian National lines in that year. The forests- that is lumber, pulp, cordwood, fence posts, and so forth-contributed 4,155,000 tons, or 28.66 per cent of the freight. Our mines contributed 3,676,000 tons, and our miscellaneous freight and manufactures contributed altogether only 17 per cent. In other words, over 80 per cent of the total freight hauled on the Canadian Northern Railway system in that year came from the farm, the forest and the mine. If you examine the figures for the Grand Trunk Pacific and the old Grand Trunk you will find they are about in that proportion. If that is a fact-and it is beyond question- it Is a sound policy to direct your fiscal system along the lines that will give the greatest encouragement to these industries. I know there are a good many of my hon. friends to my right, I think probably all'of them-and, I was going to add, I am afraid more than I should like to see among hon. gentlemen on the Governrment side of the House-who do not agree with m ' argument in this respect. But, nevertheless, I submit that it is sound business, from the fiscal point of view to shape your fiscal policy to give the greatest possible encouragement to the development of these great natural sources of wealth, and if you do that you lay the foundation for success in your manufacturing industry. There is no gainsaying that fact. No greater boon could be given to the manufacturing industries of Ontario and eastern Canada than to place one hundred and fifty or two hundred thousand good rugged farmers in western Canada, and nothing will bring more business to our factories. I submit to the Finance Minister and to the Government that when they are considering their fiscal proposals-and they are considering them now, because they are to be laid before the House next week-they could, with profit to the country, give recognition to the principle I have just laid down.
I desire to submit one other thought to the committee in this respect, and that is that these roads must be operated in such a way as to command public confidence. I believe that a way can be found to bring that about. I may say that a very great deal depends on the manner in which the Government handles the enterprise. If they absolutely, and beyond question of doubt, make it clear to the public of this country that they are animated and governed by considerations only that will bring success in opera-
Supply-Railways

tion, that they are maintaining this system free from political influences and control, they will be taking the longest possible step in establishing and maintaining, [public confidence in the system, and, from the national point of view, that is highly necessary. We have this system of railways. We cannot get rid of it. We must make the very best of it, and, consequently, that is, in my judgment, the only sound policy the Government can follow, in order to make a success of it.
I think, too, that public confidence will rest pretty largely on the fullest and most complete information that can be furnished by those in charge of the operation of the roads. I would like to see the annual report of the Canadian National system of railways made as full as possible in the information it gives to the public, as to the details of operation, the prices at which goods have been purchased, the sources where contracts have been placed, and everything else relating to the operation of the system, and to publish a sufficient number of these reports so that they can be distributed to all who wish to have them, particularly to newspapers and institutions and organizations of a public character. Let that information be diffused as widely as possible, and you will create a confidence in your system. Not only that, but you will create conditions in the public mind that will assist the Government in resisting the pressure that might involve the operation or control of these roads in political considerations. The results, I think, Mr. Chairman, in the operation of these roads for the past year are not discouraging. The hon. member from St. Antoine (Mr. Mitchell) suggested that the profits shown in the months of August, September, October and November last may have been fictitious profits. If he will reflect for a moment, I think he will find he is not correct in that statement.	*

I did not say they
were fictitious profits. I said that the operations were reduced very materially during those four months, and charged to other years under the Order in Council.
Oh no.

I certainly do not wish to do the hon. member any injustice whatever, but I distinctly gathered the impression from his remarks that he had a question mark in his own mind as to the validity of the profits shown in those months. I may be wrong in that. If I have done

him an injustice I am sorry, but I would point out to him and to the House that those four months, particularly September, October, and November, are the months of the heavy crop movement in western Canada, and there is not any doubt that the movement of the grain in western Canada provide both the National system and the Canadian Pacific system with a very large share indeed of their total earnings. It just happened this year that the movement of grain was free and heavy; it was heavier on the National lines last autumn than it was on the Canadian Pacific, and that contributed, in a very great degree, to the profits shown during those months. The results on the whole are not discouraging. I believe that, with efficient operation, with as full a knowledge on the part of the public as can be secured in regard to the potential value in these assets, we can, within a very few years, bring these roads to the point where they will more than meet their operating expenses. I would point out to the committee and to those outside of this House who are opposed to this enterprise and who are criticizing it and, I submit, not giving it a fair show or trial, that we have in these roads a splendid potential asset. If we dissipate that now; if we follow the advice that has been given in some quarters, that the Government should get rid of this system, pass it over to private hands at any price at which they will take it, what will be the result? This country will lose absolutely and forever the potential value that rests in this system to-day, but it will not escape a very large share of the liability that is in the system; it will not escape its bond guarantees; we shall lose all the cash and land grants that we have put into this system in the past, and we shall lose them forever. Those are the business considerations that should govern in the whole survey of this question. These roads are a good potential asset; if we have courage, vigour and honesty in the administration of the enterprise and I venture to say that there are many in this House who will live to see the day when they and this country will be proud of the Canadian National system of railways, I am wholly convinced that it can be made a success.
I have already expressed my opinion as to the statement brought down by the Minister of Railways. I liked the clear, definite position that he took in respect particularly to the control and management of these roads. A heavy responsibility rests upon the Government in the selection of the board that will administer

Supply-Railways
this system, in the selection of the management that will control its operation. As the minister pointed out the other day, the total amount spent by the National Railways last year involved more than $343,000,000. That is a vast sum of money; but I am convinced also that the men can be secured who will give this enterprise their undivided attention, who will bring to their work, not only a spirit of public service, but the ability and capacity to manage efficiently an enterprise of this kind. Such men can be found, and I hope and trust this Government will do everything it can to find such men. This question, let me repeat, is too grave and too great to be lightly considered. The losses are great; the responsibility is great; but I am convinced, if this enterprise is tackled vigorously, earnestly and honestly, a great success can be made of it, and in the years to come this country and even the members of this House who are now considering the matter, will have good reason for pride in our National system of railways.
Progress reported.

MEMORIAL TO THE LATE COLONEL G. H. BAKER, M.P.
speechtext:
I have the honour to inform the House that I have received a message from the Senate informing this House that the Honourable Messieurs Bradbury, Casgrain, Foster (Alma), Griesbach and Pope, have been appointed a special committee to further consider and determine the form of the memorial to be erected in the Parliament buildings to the late Lieutenant-Colonel George Harold Baker, member of Parliament for Brome, who- lost his life on the field of battle, and inviting this House to appoint a like committee to act jointly with the committee of the Senate.
At six o'clock the House adjourned without the question being put, pursuant to rule.
Thursday, May 18, 1922.
